module: Read the Act and frame an AI use case

lesson.title: What counts as an AI system
lesson.summary: Distinguish an AI system from ordinary automation and from a general-purpose model.

blocks: An **AI system** is machine-based, operates with some autonomy and infers from inputs how to generate outputs for explicit or implicit objectives. Its predictions, content, recommendations or decisions can influence physical or digital environments.
Ask what the system actually does, how it was built and where its output goes. A product being marketed as 'AI' is evidence to investigate, not a legal definition.

sources.title: AI Act, 27 July 2026 baseline: Article 3(1), 3(63), 3(66), recital 12
Commission AI-system definition guidelines C(2025) 5053 final, paragraphs 8–10, 14–23, 26–31, 46–47, 61–64; non-binding

blocks: Inference is central to the definition. Learning approaches can derive patterns from data; logic or knowledge-based approaches can infer from encoded knowledge. Ordinary sorting or arithmetic that simply executes fixed human instructions is not automatically AI.

In our fictional example, an ordinary list sorted by a specified date is different from a learned system predicting a person's suitability. Assess the actual architecture rather than relying only on the output's label.

sources.title: AI Act, 27 July 2026 baseline: Article 3(1), 3(63), 3(66), recital 12
Commission AI-system definition guidelines C(2025) 5053 final, paragraphs 8–10, 14–23, 26–31, 46–47, 61–64; non-binding

blocks: Autonomy does not mean complete independence from people. A person may submit an input while the system generates the output itself. A later human review does not, by itself, remove the system from the definition.

Adaptiveness after deployment is optional: the Act says a system may adapt. A trained system can remain an AI system even when its deployed parameters stay fixed. The Commission guidelines explain these elements but are non-binding.

sources.title: AI Act, 27 July 2026 baseline: Article 3(1), 3(63), 3(66), recital 12
Commission AI-system definition guidelines C(2025) 5053 final, paragraphs 8–10, 14–23, 26–31, 46–47, 61–64; non-binding

blocks: A **general-purpose AI model** has significant generality and can competently perform many distinct tasks and be integrated into downstream applications. A model and an AI system are related but different objects.

Northbridge integrates a model into an assistant with documents, an interface and permissions. Assess the assistant's actual function as a system. Do not copy a model-level conclusion to every application using it. Research/prototyping exclusions and model obligations require their own checks.

questions.prompt: A sales tool sorts entries by a fixed date rule. What is the sound starting point?

options.blocks: Check the definition; automation alone is insufficient
options.reason: Inference and the other definition elements need evidence.

options.blocks: Classify all automated software as AI
options.reason: Automation alone does not establish the statutory definition.

options.blocks: Classify it solely from its marketing label
options.reason: Branding cannot replace architecture and functionality evidence.

questions.prompt: A learned recommendation system never retrains after deployment. Does that fact alone exclude it?

options.blocks: Every AI system must keep retraining
options.reason: The statutory definition does not require continuing learning.

options.blocks: Human review always removes AI status
options.reason: Review does not remove the system's inference capability.
The definition uses an optional adaptation element.

questions.prompt: One general-purpose model powers a chat assistant and a separate hiring tool. What follows?

options.blocks: The interface makes model rules disappear
options.reason: System and model rules are distinct and may both matter.

options.blocks: Their system functions and contexts can differ
options.reason: A shared model does not give applications identical purposes or legal treatment.

options.blocks: Every application has the same classification
options.reason: The application and its intended use still matter.
